articles.author: Odinaka Robert Nnamani
articles.description:
Splitting a monolith into services gives you the vocabulary for free: independent, decoupled, autonomous. The architecture has to earn those words — and most don’t.
There’s a fast way to tell whether yours did. Don’t look at the deployment diagram. Look at where the contracts live.
In a gRPC system, the contracts are the .proto files: the message shapes and service definitions every service agrees to speak. They have to live somewhere, and somewhere usually means "inside whichever service was built first."
So the orders service owns the protos. The users service needs them, so it imports them straight from the orders repo. Payments needs the same messages, and rather than set up the import, someone copy-pastes the files and moves on.
orders-service/          ← .proto files live here

articles.title: Your microservices aren’t decoupled

articles.author: Panagis Tzivras
articles.description:
ARGOS : : started on a 27-inch monitor. Wide screen, mouse, keyboard, time to think. That is how you build a digital twin. It is not how you use one.
Civil protection happens in trucks, on beaches, at fire posts, in the rain. The person who needs the map is holding a phone, possibly with gloves, possibly in a hurry, possibly without a desk in sight. If the map does not work on a phone, it does not work where it matters.
v0.0.8 is the first mobile-focused release. Not a redesign. A repair of the worst friction.
What changed:
44 px touch targets. The layer toggles, the zoom buttons, the legend items. Every interactive element is now at least 44 px in both directions. No more fat-finger misses.


Layer drawer auto-dismiss. Tap the map, the drawer slides away. The map is the focus; the UI gets out of the way.


Marine slider no longer buried. The wave height slider was hiding under the legend on small screens. Now it sits above it, reachable.


Bilingual gold toast. Toggle a layer, and a small gold banner confirms: "Ενεργοποιήθηκε" in Greek, "Enabled" in English. No ambiguity about whether your tap registered.


Popup sizing. Building popups now fit within a 375 px viewport. No horizontal scroll. No clipped text.



What did not change:
The models are the same. The data is the same. The validation is the same. This is a usability pass, not a content update. The map is still a screening baseline with directional validation, not an operational forecast. The marine layer is still unvalidated. The Ithaca ferry is still not modelled.
But the map is now usable on the device you actually carry.
Test it. Open argos-geo.org/map on your phone. Toggle the wildfire layer. Tap a building. Ask the twin a question. It works. It is not perfect. It is better than last week. And next week it will be better again.
articles.title: ARGOS : : The map works on phones now

Old desktop apps and many Windows dialogs use a plain edit control …

Em Go, a convenção para testar uma função com vários casos é montar uma tabela de entradas e resultados esperados e percorrê-la com um loop. É o padrão chamado de table-driven tests. Junto com subtestes (t.Run) e execução paralela (t.Parallel), ele cobre cenários felizes, casos extremos e caminhos de erro em uma função só, e a suíte roda em uma fração do tempo sequencial.

articles.description:
Running one AI coding agent on a project is easy. Running two or three at once on the same Mac is where it gets messy. I've had Claude Code fixing a bug while Codex worked on a feature in the same repo, and an hour later I found two dev servers on two ports, a branch with both agents' changes mixed together, and test data in my local database that neither of them should have touched.
None of this is the agents' fault. They're all working in one shared place. The fix is to give each agent its own space. Here's how I set that up by hand, with plain commands, and what to clean up afterwards.
When two agents work on one project, they usually share five things:
The same branch and working tree. Both agents edit the same files on disk. One agent's half-finished change breaks the other agent's te…

articles.author: Sherotree
articles.description:
I asked an agent to “add tests for this React form.” Ten minutes later CI was green, coverage jumped 12 points, and I felt productive. Then I broke the submit handler on purpose. Every test still passed.
That’s fake green: the suite looks healthy, the badge is bright, and the product is still unprotected.
AI is great at producing tests. It’s mediocre at choosing what those tests should prove. If you don’t constrain it, you get a wall of renders, snapshots, and happy-path clicks that never touch the bug you actually ship.
I keep seeing the same patterns from agent-written suites:
Render-only tests — screen.getByText("Save") after mount. Proves the string exists, not that save works.
Implementation spies — assert useState was called, or that an internal helper ran. Refactors break the test; …
articles.title: AI-Generated Frontend Tests: Fake Green vs Real Coverage

articles.author: VelocityAI
articles.description:
My father asked me last Thanksgiving whether ChatGPT could help him draft a letter to his insurance company. I said yes, and walked him through it. Ten minutes later he closed the laptop and said, “I don’t trust it.” Not because it gave a bad answer. Because it gave a confident one, and he had no way to verify it.
My nineteen-year-old cousin, sitting across the table, looked genuinely confused. “Just ask it to cite sources,” she said. “Or ask it three different ways and see if the answers agree.” She wasn’t being dismissive. She was describing a workflow she’d developed over two years of daily use. To her, the model’s confidence was not a warning sign. It was the starting point of a verification loop she runs without thinking.
That gap is the thing I want to write about. Not the generation…
articles.title: The AI Generation Gap: Why Young People Trust Models and Older People Don't—and Why Both Are Right
